p.src: Curvature from Commutators and the Newtonian Limit

u.src: Curvature from Commutators and the Newtonian Limit
en: Curvature from Commutators and the Newtonian Limit

p.src: Curvature is easy to picture and harder to calculate. A vector carried around a small closed loop generally returns with a changed orientation, but turning that geometric statement into a usable formula requires careful notation. We shall introduce only as much operator language as is needed to make the calculation transparent. The reward is substantial: the Riemann tensor will emerge as a commutator, its contractions will lead to the Ricci tensor and scalar curvature, and the same geometric language will then meet Newtonian gravity in the weak-field limit.

p.src: The lecture has two distinct movements. The first is mathematical. We derive curvature by comparing covariant differentiation in two orders. The second is physical. We place a slowly moving particle in a weak, nearly static field and ask how the geodesic equation can reproduce $F=ma$ and Poisson’s equation. Those two movements meet in the search for a generally covariant field equation.

p.src: Vector Fields and Linear Operators

u.src: Vector Fields and Linear Operators
en: Vector Fields and Linear Operators

p.src:
Let $V^\alpha(x)
  =
  \bigl(V^0(x),V^1(x),V^2(x),V^3(x)\bigr)$ be a vector field on four-dimensional spacetime. It is useful to regard its four components as four functions collected into one column vector. Several familiar operations on this collection are linear operators.

Let $V^\alpha(x)

en:
Let $V^\alpha(x)
  =
  \bigl(V^0(x),V^1(x),V^2(x),V^3(x)\bigr)$ be a vector field on four-dimensional spacetime. It is useful to regard its four components as four functions collected into one column vector. Several familiar operations on this collection are linear operators.

p.src:
First, differentiation with respect to a coordinate is an operator: $\partial_\mu V^\alpha(x)
  =
  \frac{\partial V^\alpha(x)}{\partial x^\mu}.$ Second, multiplication by an ordinary function is an operator: $F(x)\,V^\alpha(x).$ Third, a matrix acts on the component index: $(MV)^\alpha=M^\alpha{}_\beta V^\beta.$ The matrix may itself depend on position, $M^\alpha{}_\beta=M^\alpha{}_\beta(x)$. These examples are not an exhaustive catalogue; they are exactly the ingredients needed below.

p.src:
The covariant derivative combines differentiation with a position-dependent matrix: $(\nabla_\mu V)^\alpha
  =
  \partial_\mu V^\alpha
  +
  \Gamma^\alpha{}_{\mu\beta}V^\beta.$ For each fixed value of $\mu$, define the matrix $(\Gamma_\mu)^\alpha{}_\beta
  =
  \Gamma^\alpha{}_{\mu\beta}.$ Then the same definition can be written schematically as $\boxed{\nabla_\mu=\partial_\mu+\Gamma_\mu.}$ The indices $\alpha,\beta$ are hidden matrix indices; $\mu$ labels which directional derivative and which connection matrix are being used. Whenever the compact notation becomes ambiguous, Eq.  restores all three roles.

p.src: The One Commutator Identity We Need

u.src: The One Commutator Identity We Need
en: The One Commutator Identity We Need

p.src: For two operators $A$ and $B$, their product $AB$ means that $B$ acts first and $A$ acts second. Their commutator is $=AB-BA.$ For noncommuting operators, reversing the sequence can change the result.

p.src:
Regard $F(x)$ as the operator that multiplies by the function $F$. The elementary identity needed for curvature is $\boxed{[\partial_x,F(x)]=\frac{dF}{dx}.}$ This is an operator identity, so its meaning must be tested on an arbitrary function $V(x)$: $\begin{aligned}
V
  &=
  \partial_x(FV)-F\partial_xV
  \notag\\
  &=
  \frac{dF}{dx}V
  +
  F\frac{dV}{dx}
  -
  F\frac{dV}{dx}
  \notag\\
  &=
  \frac{dF}{dx}V.
  \end{aligned}$ The terms in which the derivative acts on $V$ cancel. The remaining instruction is simply multiplication by $dF/dx$.

p.src: A Loop as a Difference of Differences

u.src: A Loop as a Difference of Differences
en: A Loop as a Difference of Differences

p.src:
Choose two infinitesimal displacement vectors, $\epsilon^\mu$ and $\eta^\nu$, spanning a small parallelogram. Label its corners $A,B,C,D$, and parallel transport a vector successively along $A\longrightarrow B\longrightarrow C\longrightarrow D
  \longrightarrow A.$ The base point returns to $A$, but the transported vector need not return with the same components. Denote the initial vector by $V_A$ and the final one by $V_A'$.

p.src: The transported vector around an infinitesimal loop. The dashed offset at $A$ records its change in orientation after the path has returned to its starting point.

u.src: The transported vector around an infinitesimal loop. The dashed offset at $A$ records its change in orientation after the path has returned to its starting point.

p.src:
The loop mismatch can be isolated by an intentionally engineered difference of differences: $\begin{aligned}
  &\bigl[(V_C-V_D)-(V_B-V_A)\bigr]
  \notag\\
  &\qquad
  -
  \bigl[(V_C-V_B)-(V_D-V_A')\bigr]
  =
  V_A-V_A'.
  \end{aligned}$ Every intermediate value cancels. The first bracket compares horizontal differences after a vertical displacement; the second compares vertical differences after a horizontal displacement. In the infinitesimal limit these become two second-order operations taken in opposite orders.

p.src:
Because the vectors at neighboring points must be compared by parallel transport, ordinary derivatives are not adequate. The finite differences become covariant derivatives. With the convention $V^\alpha
  =
  R^\alpha{}_{\beta\mu\nu}V^\beta,$ the leading holonomy around the oriented loop is $\Delta V^\alpha
  =
  R^\alpha{}_{\beta\mu\nu}
  V^\beta\epsilon^\mu\eta^\nu
  +
  O(\ell^3),$ where $\Delta V^\alpha=V_A'{}^\alpha-V_A^\alpha$ for the corresponding orientation. The characteristic edge length is $\ell$, so the leading change is of order $\ell^2$.

p.src: Expanding the Covariant-Derivative Commutator

u.src: Expanding the Covariant-Derivative Commutator
en: Expanding the Covariant-Derivative Commutator

p.src:
Insert Eq.  into the commutator: $\begin{aligned}
&=
  [\partial_\mu+\Gamma_\mu,
    \partial_\nu+\Gamma_\nu]
  \notag\\
  &=
  [\partial_\mu,\partial_\nu]
  +
  [\partial_\mu,\Gamma_\nu]
  -
  [\partial_\nu,\Gamma_\mu]
  +
  [\Gamma_\mu,\Gamma_\nu].
  \end{aligned}$ For smooth fields in a coordinate basis, $=0.$ The mixed terms are evaluated with Eq. , while the last term remains because matrix multiplication is generally noncommutative: $=
  \partial_\mu\Gamma_\nu
  -
  \partial_\nu\Gamma_\mu
  +
  \Gamma_\mu\Gamma_\nu
  -
  \Gamma_\nu\Gamma_\mu.$

p.src:
The derivative structure is equally important. Since $\Gamma\sim g^{-1}\partial g$, Eq.  contains $Riemann
  \sim
  \partial^2 g
  +
  (g^{-1}\partial g)(g^{-1}\partial g).$ Some terms contain two derivatives acting on one metric component; others are quadratic in first derivatives. If the metric is known as a function of position, the curvature is therefore determined, although the component calculation can be laborious.

p.src: Intrinsic curvature is not embedding curvature

u.src: Intrinsic curvature is not embedding curvature
en: Intrinsic curvature is not embedding curvature

p.src: A sheet of paper remains intrinsically flat when it is rolled into a cylinder. Distances and angles measured by an observer confined to the sheet have not changed, and small-loop parallel transport detects no intrinsic curvature. The rolled sheet does have extrinsic curvature because it bends inside the surrounding three-dimensional space. General relativity concerns the intrinsic geometry measured by observers living in spacetime, not how spacetime might be embedded in some larger arena.

  \qquad

p.src:
Integration determines the relation only up to a constant: $g_{00}=C+2\Phi.$ Far from an isolated source, $\Phi\to0$ and the metric approaches Minkowski spacetime, so $C=1$. Thus $\boxed{g_{00}\simeq1+2\Phi}
  \qquad(c=1).$ Restoring units gives $g_{00}\simeq1+2\Phi/c^2$.

p.src: Poisson’s Equation and the Source

u.src: Poisson’s Equation and the Source
en: Poisson’s Equation and the Source

p.src:
Let $\mathbf a(\mathbf x)$ be the Newtonian acceleration field. With the convention used above, $\mathbf a=-\boldsymbol{\nabla}\Phi.$ Gauss’s law for Newtonian gravity is $\boldsymbol{\nabla}\cdot\mathbf a
  =
  -4\pi G\rho,$ so the potential obeys Poisson’s equation: $\boxed{\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho,}
  \qquad
  \nabla^2
  =
  \partial_x^2+\partial_y^2+\partial_z^2.$

p.src:
In units $c=1$, rest-mass density is the leading contribution to energy density. In the slow-moving frame, $T_{00}\simeq T^{00}\simeq\rho.$ Poisson’s equation can therefore be written $\nabla^2\Phi
  =
  4\pi G T_{00}.$ Using $g_{00}=1+2\Phi$, the constant disappears under the Laplacian: $\boxed{\nabla^2g_{00}=8\pi G T_{00}.}$ We have learned that a metric component is controlled by an energy–momentum component. This is already the seed of the gravitational field equation.

A fundamental equation must instead equate complete tensors.

p.src: The operator notation $\nabla_\mu=\partial_\mu+\Gamma_\mu$ turns the geometric experiment of parallel transport into a calculation. A difference of differences around an infinitesimal loop is a commutator of covariant derivatives, and the resulting operator is the Riemann tensor. Its pair antisymmetries, pair exchange, and Bianchi identity determine its component structure; its mixed contractions produce the Ricci tensor and scalar curvature.

p.src: The same lecture then places the geometry under physical pressure. A slowly moving particle in a weak, nearly static field follows a geodesic whose spatial acceleration is $-\Gamma^i{}_{00}$. With signature $+---$, this identifies $g_{00}\simeq1+2\Phi$. Newtonian Poisson theory then becomes the component relation $\nabla^2g_{00}=8\pi G T_{00}$.

p.src: That component equation cannot be the final theory because it belongs to one approximation and one frame. The lecture therefore ends with a sharply posed reconstruction problem: find a symmetric two-index curvature tensor whose Newtonian limit is the component equation and whose covariant form can stand opposite $T_{\mu\nu}$. The only available combination is poised to become the Einstein tensor.
